posts.title: Document-heavy work (PDFs, Excel, email) and where AI agents actually help
posts.excerpt: A realistic look at how desktop AI agents and local tools handle repetitive document work without leaking commercial data or relying on manual copy-pasting.
posts.body:
In most Indian businesses, paperwork never really disappeared. It just turned into digital files. Instead of paper folders, your team deals with a daily flood of vendor PDFs, purchase orders, balance sheets, customer emails, and messy Excel workbooks. 

Every morning starts the same way. Someone downloads an invoice from an email, verifies the line items against an Excel tracker, checks whether the payment terms match the original agreement, and replies to confirm receipt. None of this work is difficult, but it consumes hours of focused attention. When people get tired, numbers get transposed, dates get missed, and communication stalls.

Over the past two years, many business owners tried solving this with web-based AI chatbots. The initial excitement usually wears off quickly. Copying and pasting data into a browser tab across twenty documents a day is exhausting. More importantly, pasting client contracts, financial sheets, and sensitive price lists into external websites raises serious data privacy concerns. 

To be genuinely useful for document-heavy work, AI cannot just be a text box in a browser. It has to sit where your files actually live, work across multiple steps, and protect your commercial records.

### Where web chatbots fail on documents

A standard chatbot treats every prompt in isolation. If you have an eighty-page PDF, a separate pricing spreadsheet, and an email thread with five revisions, a browser prompt struggles to keep the full context straight. You spend more time writing prompts, explaining context, and checking for hallucinations than you would spend doing the task manually.

Furthermore, document work is rarely about generating prose. It is about validation and comparison. You need to know if the total in row 42 of a sheet matches the balance listed on page three of a PDF. You need to know if a vendor has quietly altered an indemnity clause in a draft contract. These tasks require structured workflows and direct access to local files, not conversational small talk.

### How desktop-first agents change the process

adris.tech approaches this problem by running an AI office directly on your Windows desktop. The entire application runs on your own machine. It connects to the AI models you choose, whether you prefer using a free key from NVIDIA or Groq, your own API key from Gemini, OpenAI, or Anthropic, your Claude Code or Codex subscription, or local open models running completely offline.

Here is how the modules inside adris.tech handle the heavy lifting of daily documentation:

1. **Shared context with Brain**: Instead of re-explaining your company background, standard operating terms, or vendor lists in every conversation, Brain maintains a shared local knowledge graph. When you analyze a new document, the agents can cross-reference it against the context stored in your local knowledge graph.

2. **Targeted review with Guard**: Contracts and formal agreements demand careful scrutiny. Guard is designed for contract review, phishing checks, and vulnerability briefings. Before anyone signs a modified vendor agreement, Guard can review the text to identify unusual liabilities, changes in standard payment timelines, or missing protections.

3. **Multi-agent collaboration in Krew**: With 57 specialist AI agents available in Krew, different agents can tackle different sides of a problem. One agent can review structured data, while another drafts a formal clarification response. Because this happens in one unified window, you do not need to switch between five different tabs or separate software tools.

4. **Structured steps with Automation**: Visual workflows let you outline recurring tasks step by step. Rather than manually opening files and running individual prompts, you can set up workflows that process documents through specific checks in sequence.

5. **Complete privacy with Models and Vault**: If you handle confidential client records, you can switch to the Models module, which supports about 51 local open models. Because local models process text on your hardware without sending tokens outside, your documents remain strictly on your machine. Meanwhile, Vault provides DNS-level blocking for ads, trackers, and malware to keep your environment clean.

### When you need something built for your exact pipeline

The free version of adris.tech includes all these modules: Krew, Automation, Coder, Models, Vault, Guard, Mesh (which pools RAM across machines), and Brain. It costs nothing, with no hidden tiers or subscriptions.

However, some businesses operate with highly customized document formats, proprietary internal databases, or complex multi-department approval chains. A custom build can provide an agentic AI office created specifically around your business rules, file structures, and everyday workflows, scoped and agreed in writing before any work begins.

Document work does not have to be an endless cycle of manual cross-referencing. When your tools run locally and work together, routine document handling becomes orderly, private, and fast.

posts.title: How a small Indian manufacturer can automate enquiry-to-quotation with AI agents
posts.excerpt: A practical walkthrough of using local AI agents to turn incoming purchase enquiries into accurate quotations without adding headcount.
posts.body:
## The enquiry-to-quotation bottleneck

Most small manufacturers in India run the same loop: a WhatsApp message or email arrives with a vague request, "need 500 pcs of M8 bolts, SS304, delivered to Pune." Someone reads it, checks stock in a spreadsheet or ERP, asks the shop floor about capacity, calculates material cost plus conversion, adds freight and GST, types a quote in Word or Excel, emails it back, then follows up three days later. Multiply this by twenty enquiries a day and the owner or sales person spends half their time on paperwork instead of production.

## What changes when the loop runs on your own machine

adris.tech is a free Windows desktop app that brings a team of AI agents and the tools they need into one window. It runs locally, uses your own AI keys (Groq, NVIDIA, Gemini, OpenAI, Anthropic, or a local model), and costs nothing. No cloud subscription, no data leaving your premises. You install it, add your keys, and the agents start working.

For enquiry-to-quotation, three modules matter most: **Krew** (specialist agents), **Automation** (visual workflows), and **Vault** (DNS-level blocking so the machine stays clean).

## Step 1: Capture every enquiry in one place

Create a **Mail Watcher** agent in Krew. Point it at your sales inbox (IMAP) or the WhatsApp Business API webhook. The agent reads each message, extracts: part number or drawing reference, quantity, material grade, delivery pincode, and any special terms (packing, certification, payment). It writes a structured row into a local SQLite table, no cloud database needed.

## Step 2: Enrich with internal data

Add a **Stock Checker** agent. Give it read access to your ERP export (CSV, Excel, or direct DB if you allow). The agent matches the enquiry line items against current stock, open purchase orders, and work-in-progress. It tags each line: *in stock*, *can make in 3 days*, *needs raw material*, *out of capacity*.

## Step 3: Price it

A **Pricing Engine** agent takes the enriched row. It pulls your master price list, applies your markup rules (material + conversion + overhead + freight slab for the pincode + GST), and outputs a line-item quote. If a line is *needs raw material*, the agent fetches the latest vendor quote from your approved supplier sheet and adds lead time.

## Step 4: Generate the quotation document

A **Document Builder** agent uses a Word template stored locally. It fills in: buyer name, GSTIN, line items, totals, terms, validity, and your bank details. Saves the file as PDF in a dated folder on your machine. No manual copy-paste.

## Step 5: Send and track

An **Outreach** agent emails the PDF from your Outlook or Gmail account (SMTP) with a standard covering note. It logs the sent date, quote number, and expiry in the same SQLite table. A **Follow-up** agent wakes up on day 3 and day 7: if the quote status is still *open*, it sends a polite nudge and notifies you on the desktop.

## Wiring it together in Automation

Open the **Automation** tab. Drag the five agents onto the canvas. Connect: Mail Watcher → Stock Checker → Pricing Engine → Document Builder → Outreach → Follow-up. Set the trigger: *new row in enquiry table*. Hit **Run**. The workflow executes end-to-end on your PC. You see each step's output in the log pane. If something looks off, say, a freight slab missing, you edit the Pricing Engine's rule sheet (a simple CSV) and re-run just that node.

## Keeping data private

All of this runs inside adris. The **Vault** module blocks telemetry, tracker, and malware domains at the DNS level, so the machine only talks to the AI endpoints you configured (Groq, local Ollama, etc.). Your enquiry data, pricing logic, and customer list never leave the shop floor.

## What the owner actually does

- Reviews the daily summary email at 9 AM: "12 quotes sent, 3 pending raw material, 1 capacity clash."
- Opens the adris window, clicks the capacity clash, sees the shop floor load chart, decides to outsource or reschedule.
- Updates the vendor price CSV when a supplier revises rates.
- Adds a new markup rule in the Pricing Engine when GST slabs change.

No coding. No new hires. The agents handle the repetitive reading, matching, calculating, formatting, and chasing. You handle the exceptions.

## Start small, expand later

Begin with one product line, say, fasteners. Get the workflow stable for two weeks. Then clone the Automation canvas for fittings, then for fabricated assemblies. Each canvas reuses the same agents; only the rule sheets and templates differ.

## When the standard flow isn't enough

If your process needs a custom integration, pulling BOMs from SolidWorks, pushing quotes into Tally, checking vendor portals for live stock, that is a custom build. We scope it in writing, build the agents and workflows inside your adris install, and hand over the source.

**Ready to automate your enquiry-to-quotation flow? Request a custom build at https://www.adris.tech/contact?type=custom_build**

posts.title: Your client's contract is not your data to upload
posts.excerpt: Every AI contract reviewer asks you to upload the document first. If you handle other people’s agreements, that is a decision with someone else’s name on it.
posts.body:
There is a step in almost every AI contract review tool that nobody wants to talk about. Before you get a single insight, you upload the document.

For a personal lease, fine. For a client's master services agreement, it is a decision with someone else's name on it.

## What you are actually agreeing to

When a contract goes to a cloud reviewer, three things become true at once. The counterparty's commercial terms sit on a third party's servers. Your client's name and pricing sit there with them. And the terms under which they sit there are written by a company that is not you and can change them.

Most of those terms are reasonable. Some permit processing for service improvement. Almost all of them require you, if you are handling client data, to add that provider to a processor list you may have told your client was shorter.

The practical problem is not that the provider is untrustworthy. It is that you have taken on a disclosure obligation in exchange for a faster read of a PDF.

## The version of this that has no step

Run the analysis where the file already is. The document is read on your machine, the clauses are graded there, and nothing is transmitted.

There is no upload to disclose, no processor to add, and no retention policy to read — because there is no third party in the sentence. When a client asks where their agreement went, the answer is nowhere.

## What a useful review looks like

A tool that says "this contract is risky" has told you nothing you can act on. The findings worth having name the section, quote the sentence, and say in plain language what it means for you:

- **Auto-renewal traps** — rolls over for another 24 months unless cancelled inside a short window, often with an uncapped price rise
- **Unlimited liability on your side** while theirs is capped at fees paid
- **No termination right**, or one that costs the full remaining term
- **IP assignment** where you thought you were licensing
- **One-way indemnities** covering costs outside your control

Quoted, they are something you can take back to the other side. Unquoted, they are a score you have to trust.

---

We built this into [Guard](/modules/guard), and wrote up how it works on the [contract review](/contract-review-software) page. It runs locally, and the free tier includes enough scans to test it on an agreement you already signed — which is the honest way to evaluate it.

posts.title: Running a local model stopped being a hobby project
posts.excerpt: Two years ago this meant Docker, CUDA errors and a weekend. What changed is not the models — it is that the boring parts finally got solved.
posts.body:
The first time most people try to run a model locally, they download something far too large for their machine and watch everything freeze. They conclude local AI is not ready. It is a reasonable conclusion from the evidence, and it is out of date.

## What actually changed

Not the models, mostly. Small open models were already decent. What changed is that the setup stopped being a project:

- Quantised weights mean a genuinely useful model fits in a few gigabytes rather than tens
- Runtimes handle the hardware detection you used to do by hand
- The gap between a 7B model and a frontier one closed enough that, for summarising a document or drafting a reply, you often cannot tell

The remaining problem is not capability. It is that nothing tells you *which* model your computer can actually run before you spend twenty minutes downloading one.

## The question worth answering first

How much memory do you have free, right now, and which models fit in it comfortably rather than technically?

That is a boring question and it is the one that decides whether your first attempt works. We put it at the front: the catalogue reads your available memory and marks each model comfortable, tight, or out of reach before you commit to the download.

Eight gigabytes of RAM runs a small model fine. Sixteen is comfortable for mid-size. No GPU is required — it makes things faster, it is not a condition of entry.

## What it is good for, honestly

Local models are excellent at the high-volume, low-glamour work: reading documents, extracting fields, classifying, summarising, drafting a first pass. That is most of what an automation actually does.

They are not the right tool for everything, and pretending otherwise is how people end up disappointed. For hard reasoning you will still reach for a frontier model — which is why connecting your own API key sits right next to the local option rather than being hidden.

The difference is that once the weights are on your disk, running them costs nothing per use. That changes what is worth automating: things you would never send to a metered API become obvious once each run is free.

posts.title: Scanning Secrets with TruffleHog: A Practical Guide for Small Businesses
posts.excerpt: Repository: https://github.com/trufflesecurity/trufflehog · facts checked on GitHub 24 Oct 2026.
posts.body:
## The hidden risk of leaked credentials
Organizations often store code, configuration files and operational logs in places that are easy to access. When a secret such as an API key or database password is unintentionally written to a repository or a chat channel it can be harvested by attackers. Finding those secrets before they are abused is a core requirement for any security program.

## What it is
TruffleHog is an open source secret scanning tool maintained by Truffle Security. It is released under the AGPL 3.0 licence. Its latest release is v3.99.6 on 24 Oct 2026. The project has 28,676 stars on GitHub as of 24 Oct 2026.

## What it finds
The scanner looks for credentials across many sources including Git repositories, chat platforms, wikis, log files, API testing services, object stores and local filesystems. It can recognise more than 800 types of secrets ranging from cloud provider keys to database passwords and private encryption keys. For each finding it tries to classify the secret to its originating service and can optionally validate whether the credential is still active.

## How a small business would use it
A web agency could run TruffleHog against client repositories before deployment to ensure no development keys are left in the code base. A clinic that manages a patient portal could scan its configuration files and server logs to verify that database passwords are not exposed. A startup building a mobile app could integrate the tool into its CI pipeline to stop accidental commits of third‑party API keys.

## Trying it
For macOS users the tool can be installed with a package manager:
```bash
brew install trufflehog
```
The Docker image can be used on any platform. A basic scan of a GitHub organization looks like:
```bash
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/pwd" trufflesecurity/trufflehog:latest github --org=trufflesecurity
```
Scanning a single repository is performed with:
```bash
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/pwd" trufflesecurity/trufflehog:latest github --repo https://github.com/trufflesecurity/test_keys
```

## Limits
The scanner cannot guarantee that every secret is malicious; it may report false positives that require human judgement. Validation of a secret relies on the ability to connect to the target service, which may be blocked by firewalls or require additional credentials. The tool does not replace secure development practices such as using environment variables or secret management solutions. Continuous monitoring and periodic manual review are still necessary.

## The skull take
TruffleHog gives small teams a fast way to locate hidden credentials in code and configuration. Run it regularly in CI and before any release to catch accidental exposure early.
